# Fuels, emissions and Euro standards {#sec-fuels-emissions}


::: {.cell}

:::


Much of the interest in vehicle data comes from its environmental questions:
how fast the fleet is moving to electric, how many older polluting vehicles
remain, and what this means for carbon emissions and air quality. This chapter
explains the fuel and emissions information in the data and its limits.

## Fuel types

| Fuel | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Petrol** and **diesel** | Conventional internal combustion engines |
| **Hybrid electric** | A petrol or diesel engine with an electric motor and battery. *Mild* hybrids use a small motor to assist the engine; *full* hybrids (such as the Toyota Prius) can drive short distances on electricity alone. Neither can be plugged in: the battery is charged by the engine and by braking |
| **Plug-in hybrid electric** (PHEV) | A hybrid with a larger battery that can be charged from the mains, giving a useful electric-only range, typically 20–50 miles |
| **Range-extended electric** | An electric vehicle with a small engine that only charges the battery |
| **Battery electric** (BEV) | Electric only, charged from the mains, with no engine |
| **Fuel cell** | Electric drive powered by a hydrogen fuel cell; very rare |
| **Gas** | Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), compressed or liquefied natural gas (CNG, LNG); usually conversions of petrol or diesel vehicles |

"Electric vehicle" is used loosely. Policy often groups battery electric,
plug-in hybrid and range-extended vehicles as *plug-in vehicles*, or uses
*ultra low emission vehicle* (ULEV) for vehicles emitting under 75g of CO~2~
per km. Always check which definition a statistic uses.

### How fuel is recorded

The DVSA and the DVLA each record a fuel, using different labels, and neither
distinguishes a plug-in hybrid from any other hybrid: DVSA records
`Hybrid Electric (Clean)` for mild, full and plug-in petrol hybrids alike. DfT's
vehicle licensing statistics do distinguish them, by model.

CARS keeps both supplied fuels (`fuel_DVSA`, `fuelType_DVLA`) and builds a
harmonised `fuel` from them: the DVSA fuel, corrected where the DVLA record or
the engine size shows it is wrong (for example a Toyota Prius recorded as
`Electric`), and with plug-in hybrids identified from DfT's records for the
vehicle's model (@sec-pipeline). `fuel_simple` groups it into six:


::: {#tbl-fuel-simple .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Vehicles in the CARS vehicle table by fuel group, all years and all vehicle types.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|fuel_simple             |   Vehicles| Share|
|:-----------------------|----------:|-----:|
|Petrol                  | 52,100,086| 55.8%|
|Diesel                  | 33,499,694| 35.9%|
|Hybrid Electric         |  3,696,925|  4.0%|
|Electric                |  2,741,613|  2.9%|
|Plug-in Hybrid Electric |  1,089,905|  1.2%|
|Other                   |    224,018|  0.2%|


:::
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: plug-in hybrids are undercounted"}
A vehicle is identified as a plug-in hybrid only when its model, as DfT
records it, is clearly a plug-in. Models sold both as plug-in and ordinary
hybrids (a BMW X1 or a Kia Niro whose model text does not say which) are left
as ordinary hybrids. The plug-in count is therefore a **lower bound**, and the
hybrid count correspondingly too high.
:::

## Engine size

Engine size is the capacity of the engine's cylinders in cubic centimetres
(cc). It is a rough guide to a vehicle's power and fuel use. A battery electric
vehicle has no engine: in the harmonised `engine_cc` its engine size is 0, and
tables that band engine size give it its own band.

## CO~2~ emissions

The CO~2~ figure (`co2`, in grams per kilometre) is the official value measured
when the model was type approved, not a measurement of the individual vehicle.
It is recorded because vehicle tax for cars registered since March 2001 depends
on it, so it is mostly missing for older vehicles.

::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: two test procedures"}
CO~2~ figures were measured on the NEDC laboratory test until it was replaced by
the more realistic WLTP test, from September 2017 for new models and September
2018 for all new cars. WLTP figures are typically higher for the same vehicle,
so a rise in recorded CO~2~ around 2018 is partly an artefact of the change of
test. Official figures also understate real-world emissions, by different
amounts in different periods.
:::

A recorded CO~2~ of zero is only kept for vehicles with no engine; elsewhere it
is treated as missing (@sec-pipeline).

## Euro emission standards

Euro standards limit the air pollutants a new vehicle may emit: nitrogen
oxides (NO~x~), particulate matter, carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons. (They do
not limit CO~2~.) Each new standard is stricter than the last, and applies to
new type approvals first and, a year or so later, to every new vehicle
registered.

- Standards for **cars, vans and motorcycles** are written in Arabic numerals:
  Euro 1 to Euro 6. Euro 6 has sub-stages (6b, 6c, 6d-TEMP, 6d, 6e) that
  tightened testing, including real driving emissions (RDE) tests on the road.
- Standards for **lorries and buses** are written in Roman numerals: Euro I to
  Euro VI. They are separate regulations measured on a different basis.

The CARS column `euro_standard` puts both on one numeric scale (1 to 6), which
is convenient, but a Euro 6 car and a Euro VI bus meet different limits.

### Recorded and assumed Euro status

The DVLA records a Euro status for only a minority of vehicles, mostly those
registered since about 2018. Because standards became compulsory on fixed
dates, though, a vehicle registered new after a standard became compulsory must
meet at least that standard. CARS uses this to fill in a Euro status where none
is recorded, and marks such values with `euro_status_src = 'euro_schedule'`.


::: {#tbl-euro-fill .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Where the Euro status of vehicles in the CARS vehicle table comes from, by body type.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}

|Light goods vehicles |  9,370,852|                         4,531,635|         4,371,296|   467,921|
|Motorcycles          |  4,020,776|                           721,776|         2,388,310|   910,690|
|(none)               |  2,922,885|                             7,473|                 0| 2,915,412|

::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: most Euro statuses are inferred"}
An assumed Euro status is the *minimum* the vehicle must meet; it may meet a
newer one. It is wrong for used imports and rebuilt vehicles, which are
registered in the UK long after they were built. If your analysis depends on
Euro status, check how much of it is recorded (`euro_status_src = 'dvla'`) and
test whether your results change without the assumed values.
:::

## Clean Air Zones and low emission zones

Several UK cities charge or restrict the most polluting vehicles in Clean Air
Zones (CAZ), and London has its Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ). The usual
minimum standards are **Euro 4 for petrol** cars and vans, **Euro 6 for diesel**
cars and vans, and **Euro VI** for buses, coaches and lorries.

Because recorded Euro status was so sparse, the CARS churn tables (Set 7,
@sec-aggregate-tables) use the vehicle's first-use date as a proxy: petrol
vehicles first used before 2006, and diesel vehicles first used before 2015, are
counted as likely non-compliant.
